annotations.text:
Same quote in all three: Highfield ADV 700 hull, Yamaha F250 motor, Dunbier trailer, five decisions, one refusal shown with its reason, $128,108 drive away.

They differ on structure and surface, not on content. All three use the app's real accent (#0a5fc2), ink (#081b2e) and faces (Inter / IBM Plex Mono / Archivo) — so what you are picking is the shape of the screen, not the palette.

Static mockups, not clickable.

A — THE HULL. Dark, photographic, one boat filling the screen. The decisions live in a rail on the right; the price is a solid white bar under everything.

Why: makes a $128k purchase feel like a $128k purchase, and it is the only one a customer would want to look at over the salesperson's shoulder.

Cost: a dark photographic screen is hostile to the dense reading a dealer does all day, and the photo takes 60% of the width to say one thing you already know.

B — THE SHEET. Light, layered white cards on a soft grey, generous spacing, the price floating in a pill.

Why: instantly legible, calm, nothing to learn. The card boundaries do the grouping so the five decisions never run together.

Cost: whitespace is paid for in density — fewer options visible at once, more scrolling on a real 40-motor list. And it looks like every other SaaS tool; it wins no argument on its own.

C — THE LEDGER. Three columns: the five decisions as a permanent spine, the open decision as a real table, and a running itemised ledger that always shows what the total is made of.

Why: the price is never a surprise, and refusals sit in the table where the choice would have been, with the reason — 'Over the hull's rating. The ADV 700 is plated to 250 hp.' It extends Quiet Precision rather than replacing it.

Cost: the least immediately impressive of the three. It asks the dealer to read, and it gives the boat 82px of height.
